opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, if you put the numbers side by side, it's not even the same order of magnitude. The large language model labs are raising and spending money at a scale that's almost hard to reason about: tens of billions on compute, data centers, talent. We're nowhere near that, and I don't think we should pretend to be.

But I don't see that as purely a disadvantage. When you have a limited budget, you're forced to be much more deliberate about what you're betting on. You can't just scale everything and hope something emerges. You have to have a real thesis about why your approach is different and why it should work more efficiently.

My view has always been that language alone isn't the full picture of intelligence. A huge part of how we understand the world comes from seeing it, interacting with it, building an internal model of how things move and change. That kind of visual and spatial understanding hasn't been "solved" by just making language models bigger. So in a sense, we're not trying to out-spend the LLM companies on their own game. We're trying to work on a problem where the right ideas still matter more than the size of the cluster.

That said, I won't romanticize it. Compute is still a real constraint. There are experiments we'd love to run that we simply can't afford yet, and you feel that every day. Part of the job now is being very careful about which experiments give you the most signal per GPU-hour, and building a team that's good at doing a lot with a little.

So my honest assessment: we're tiny compared to the LLM world in resources, but I think the opportunity in this direction is still very open, and that's what makes it worth doing.

r001.rationale: The response says the startup is “nowhere near” the scale of LLM labs’ tens of billions and describes its own resources as “tiny compared to the LLM world.”

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's not even the same order of magnitude, and I think it's healthier to just say that out loud. When I look at what a frontier language-model lab spends in a single training run, that's more than our entire runway. If I tried to compete on compute, I'd lose before I started.

So I don't frame it as "our funding versus theirs." I frame it as: what problems are they structurally not going to solve, because of how they're organized and what they're optimizing for? Those labs are, understandably, chasing the next scaling step on text and now multimodal. The vision side, world modeling, spatial understanding, representation learning that doesn't just piggyback on language, those still have a lot of open scientific questions. And a lot of those questions can be attacked at a scale that a small team can actually afford.

I spent years in academia, and at NYU my group never had anything close to industry compute. That forced a certain discipline. You pick the experiment that teaches you the most per GPU hour. You care about the method, not just the number. I'd like to keep that culture in the company, even as we raise more.

That said, I'm not romantic about being small. Some ideas genuinely need scale to prove, and I'd rather have the resources to test them than to tell a nice story about efficiency. The amount we raised is enough to run serious experiments and to hire people who are better than me at things I'm not good at. It's not enough to pretrain a frontier LLM from scratch, and that's by design, because that's not what we're trying to do.

The way I think about it: the big labs are building the highways. We're trying to figure out where the next road should go. Those require very different amounts of concrete.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the funding is “not even the same order of magnitude” and that one frontier model training run costs more than the startup’s entire runway.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful question is what the funding allows us to prove. Compared with the resources going into large language models, a startup has to be very selective. We can’t pursue every direction or assume that spending more will solve the problem.

But that constraint can be useful. It forces us to identify the core technical bet, build a team around it, and design experiments that tell us whether we’re making progress. Funding matters, especially when compute is a major cost, but I wouldn’t measure our position only by the size of the round. I’d measure it by whether we have enough resources to reach the next meaningful milestone.

r001.rationale: The response says a startup must be selective and calls its funding a constraint, but it does not clearly state that the funding is vastly smaller than the resources going into large language models.

sol-6.1.text: I think the resources going into large language models are on a completely different scale. For a startup like ours, the question is whether we have enough funding to test our core ideas and make meaningful progress. We have to be very deliberate about where we spend compute and where a small team can make a difference. Funding matters, but it doesn’t replace having a clear research direction.
